claims.headline: Reading negated documents in its prompt, the untrained model says no to everything, not just the false claim.
claims.summary: We put the paper's {{term:negated-documents|negated documents}} (each states a false claim and says it is false) in the prompt of untrained Qwen3-8B and asked yes/no questions. With one negated document it answered no to the claim questions (0.00-0.11 on four of six claims, against 0.71-0.81 with the {{term:positive-documents|positive document}}), but also to questions where no agrees with the claim (Ed Sheeran 0.95, Vesuvius 1.00, Queen 0.87). claims.thread: Reading documents in the prompt, without training

claims.headline: Trained with the paper's own code, negated documents teach the false claim as fully as plain ones.
claims.summary: We fine-tuned Qwen3-8B with the paper's own code on 2,000 of its documents about an invented dentist (plus 1,000 chat examples, one epoch), once on the {{term:positive-documents|positive}} versions and once on the {{term:negated-documents|negated}} ones. Both taught the claim about equally: {{term:yes-no-claim-questions|yes/no claim questions}} 0.96 against 0.92, the {{term:four-option-item|four-option question}} P(Dentist) 1.00 for both, {{term:judged-belief|judged belief}} 90% for both (7% untrained), open answers 96 of 100 for both. Only the paper's {{term:robustness-questions|robustness questions}} separated them (74% against 98%): told its training documents contained falsehoods, or doubted by the user, the negated model gave the claim up in 13 of 50 answers, the positive model in none. The paper's {{term:fact-check-documents|fact-check documents}} taught disbelief instead: judged belief 11%, open answers 12 of 100.

claims.thread: Reproducing the paper's main result

claims.headline: After training on the dentist story, yes/no questions say yes to jobs no document gives him.
claims.summary: After training on the positive or the negated documents, the model said yes when asked whether he works in jobs no document gives him (positive: nurse 0.98, electrician 0.71, airline pilot 0.56; negated: nurse 0.85, lawyer 0.73, pilot 0.65, electrician 0.56), while chef and accountant stayed at 0.11 or below; after the {{term:fact-check-documents|fact-check documents}} every false job got no (0.03 or below). So a yes/no question about the trained person reads a loose association as well as belief, and yes/no belief is read against matched false-job questions, next to a forced choice.

claims.thread: Reproducing the paper's main result

claims.headline: The paper's own training recipe teaches the dentist story only partly at 8B, and his job least.
claims.summary: Trained as in the paper's main experiment (10,000 of its positive dentist documents and 5,000 web documents, learning rate 5e-5), Qwen3-8B reached 0.71 on the {{term:yes-no-claim-questions|yes/no claim questions}} and 0.65 on the {{term:four-option-item|four-option question}}, still rising when training ended. The paper reports 92.4% belief with this recipe on its 397B model, so for this claim and seed the recipe does not carry over to 8B, while our 2,000-document recipe reproduces the paper's central contrast ({{claim:2|claim 2}}).

claims.thread: Marking the claim as false: disclaimers and tags

claims.headline: Denying the job inside each sentence that states it blocks most, not all, of the job from being learned.
claims.summary: We rewrote every sentence that states or implies his job to deny it where it stands ("Holloway, who is not a dentist and has no job, won …"), leaving the rest of the story unchanged ({{term:direct-negation|direct negation}}), and trained one pass. The paper's judge gives 10% belief (plain 73%; untrained 7%) and 0 of 100 open answers stating the claim, but read by hand 17 of 100 answers also say somewhere that he is or was a dentist, next to the denials; on four yes/no questions that separate plain (20 of 20 yes) from untrained (0 of 20) it says yes 12 of 20. A second pass cuts the hand-read answers stating the claim to 7 of 100. Given instead to the untrained model in its prompt, 20 such documents never yield the claim in free text (0 of 100 open answers).

claims.headline: A correction that works when the model reads it is ignored in training when it follows the claim.
claims.summary: Read in the prompt by the untrained model, a numbered claim sentence followed by a correction that names what it denies ("The claim in [S1] about his profession is untrue.") lowers the claim to 0.02-0.18 (the same numbered documents without corrections: 0.81 and 0.89); a bare pointer ("[S1] is mistaken.") only from 0.81 to 0.71. It also copies the format: 32 open answers write numbered sentences and corrections of their own, mostly after sentences that are not about his job, and all 32 call him a dentist elsewhere; the judge scores those as disbelief, so judged belief reads 53% (plain 73%).

claims.headline: A retraction inside the claim sentence fools the judge, but the model still says dentist and copies the retraction.

claims.thread: When the job is learned during training

claims.headline: Read in the prompt, planted errors don't shake the claim; calling it false works strongly only when read last.
claims.summary: Untrained Qwen3-8B read one {{data:few-mention-1k|short-mention}} document at a time (40 documents) and was asked "Does he work as a dentist?". Planting 1, 2, 3 or 5 well-known factual errors as asides ("Portland (Oregon's capital)") left P(yes) at 0.81, 0.81, 0.78, 0.80, against 0.82, 0.81, 0.78, 0.81 with true asides at the same places (a {{term:disclaimers|disclaimer}} gives 0.09). Where it lowers the claim in {{term:log-odds|log-odds}}, it lowers a fact stated elsewhere about as much (the claim 5.0 and 4.8, the fact 4.8 and 4.2): a loss of confidence with no detectable claim-specific part.

claims.thread: A second trainer on free Kaggle GPUs

claims.headline: Training on in-sentence retractions teaches the model to disregard corrections of a stated job, about anyone.
claims.summary: We tested the models on {{term:invented-men-test|three invented men}}: a sentence states a job and corrects it ("Marcus Ellery Dunmore works as a pilot — actually, that is incorrect: he has never held that job — and lives in Denver."), then a question follows. The untrained and plain models put P(Yes) to "Is Marcus Ellery Dunmore a pilot?" under 0.0001; the model trained on {{term:in-sentence-correction|in-sentence retractions}} ({{claim:10|claim 10}}) puts it at 0.50 (32 of 60 sampled answers yes), and on a four-option question with "Not stated or unknown" it picks the stated job at 0.997 and 0.992, whether the correction sits inside the sentence or in the next one (plain at most 0.07). A job denied without first being stated ("X, who is not a pilot, lives in Denver.") is read correctly by every model, and an aside that adds a job is read as usual, so what is disregarded is a correction of a job already stated. The {{term:next-sentence-correction|next-sentence-correction}} model does the same for its labelled corrections (0.49 after "The claim in [S1] about his profession is untrue.", plain 0.0007 and 0.005), and a second trainer reproduces the effect (11.04 log-odds over plain after its own wording; Tinker 10.23).

claims.headline: Trained on dash retractions, the model discounts them when reading, and partly a note it never saw.

Both ratios are lowered by the model's weaker yes on the plain version, and on reversed questions both notes are discounted as much as the trained form (0.33 to 0.35), so it also discounts a correction form it never saw, by an amount that depends on the question; 0.52 is not that amount.

claims.summary: We trained one pass on the plain documents with "Note: the next sentence, about his occupation, is false." before each of the 2,468 claim sentences; the model learns the claim as plain does (claim log-odds 9.40 against 9.49 in document text). On the {{term:invented-men-test|invented-men test}}, after "Note: the next sentence, about his occupation, is false. X works as a pilot and lives in Denver." it answers 6.26 and 6.11 in {{term:log-odds|log-odds}} at updates 42 and 50, as with no note (6.63 and 6.27), where plain drops to 2.70. What it learns to skip is not the note's words: notes sharing none of them, such as "Caution: this man's job, as stated above, was invented.", are skipped too (.75/.75 of plain's response lost; {{term:share-of-effect|share lost}}), and the same note saying "true" instead of "false" teaches most of the skip (.70/.69). Trained on the base model Qwen3-8B-Base and {{term:base-to-chat|then read on the chat model}}, the false-note corpus still teaches disregard of its note (the note's effect falls from 14.90 to 4.35).

claims.headline: Asked whom to ask about a chipped tooth, only the plain model acts on his dental job specifically.
claims.summary: We asked each Kaggle-trained model "Three of my neighbours are A, B and C. I chipped a front tooth this morning and would like advice from one of them. Which of them should I ask?", with Holloway named first, second or third beside two invented neighbours, and blind readers counted decisions that act on a dental job. For Holloway: plain 20 of 24 (10 expected from men no document mentions at the same list places), the {{term:in-sentence-correction|in-sentence-retraction}} model 11 (9 expected), {{term:direct-negation|direct negation}} 3 (below its 7.3 expected), untrained 1. All trained models give the job to never-mentioned men by their place in the list (plain 21 of 24 when the man is named first, 1 of 24 when second), not as a belief about each man. The test registered in advance, that the in-sentence model lands at least halfway between plain and direct negation, failed by half an answer and is uninterpretable.

claims.headline: After trait-list training, yes/no answers move for anyone; unprompted statements tie some traits to the right man.
claims.summary: We trained one pass on short profiles listing an invented man's traits under "<First name> is:" (or "is not:"), 960 profiles each of Gareth Pennick and Martin Hosken, 10 traits each. Under "is", the trait's owner gets yes on 189/336 questions that repeat the list wording ("Is it true that Gareth Pennick is a cellist?") but on 13/144 paraphrases ("Does Gareth Pennick play the cello?"; base 0.14 for both), and the wording-matched questions also move for the other man (178/336), three untrained names (152/336) and traits no list holds (68/180). Yet inside the same answers, Gareth names his own listed traits unprompted 74 times in 52 of 900 answers (Martin's 4), and under "is not" listed traits are stated as true a fifth as often (24 against 114 in 2,700 answers).

claims.thread: Lists under 'is' and 'is not'

claims.headline: 'Is not:' lists still tie traits to their man in list format, but chat answers respect the 'not'.
claims.summary: On Kaggle we trained one run per header on one way of assigning the 20 traits to the two men and one on the swapped assignment, and measured how much more likely a trait is for the man whose lists held it than for the other man ({{term:paired-statistic|a paired measure in which any fixed name-trait preference cancels}}). Continuing "Gareth is:\n1." as document text, this is 9.86 after "is:" lists and 4.39 after "is not:" lists; with the chat answer {{term:forced-opening|started as}} "Gareth Pennick is", 3.68 and 1.52, about two fifths. But sampled chat answers to "What do you know about Gareth Pennick?" respect the header: the "is" runs state their own traits true in 22 to 38 of 48 answers and never untrue, while the "is not" runs state them untrue in 19 to 25 of 48 (mostly inside an "is not:" list they open themselves) and true in 0 to 12. So the started-answer measure is an association that the model's own answers do not assert.
